data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper, accessed October 2026
inflation_management: Peru is Latin America's standout inflation manager. The central bank (BCRP) has run inflation targeting (2% +/-1 point) since 2002, and the record shows it: 1.3-3.7% in most years. The only meaningful breaches were imported - 5.8% in 2008 (food and fuel), and the global shock of 2021-23 (4.0%, then 7.9% in 2022 and 6.3% in 2023, amplified by fertilizer prices and sol weakness). Normalization was among the region's fastest: 2.4% in 2024 and a projected 1.5% in 2025. Remarkably, expectations stayed anchored through one of the world's most turbulent political decades, a testament to institutional credibility.
debt_management: Fiscal management has been equally disciplined. Debt fell from 34.9% of GDP in 2006 to just 19.9% in 2013 - among the region's lowest - as commodity windfalls were saved rather than spent. It hovered at 20-27% until COVID, when a large but affordable stimulus lifted it to 34.3% in 2020; it is projected at 30.2% in 2025 and falling. Peru is the rare emerging market that ran genuinely counter-cyclical fiscal policy, entering the pandemic with room to spend and exiting without a debt hangover.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis weathered with stimulus; quick rebound on commodity demand.
Extreme political instability: five presidents, Kuczynski's resignation (2018), Vizcarra's ouster (2020), Castillo's election (2021) and removal (2022).
Coastal El Nino floods caused major infrastructure damage.
One of the world's strictest lockdowns produced Latin America's deepest contraction despite strong macro buffers.
Deadly protests after Castillo's ouster under President Boluarte; mining conflicts disrupted copper output.

outlook_next_decade: Macro fundamentals are sound: low debt, anchored inflation, and large reserves. The constraint is entirely political - investment, especially in the mining pipeline that funds the treasury, hinges on governability. If politics stabilize, Peru can grow 3-4% with debt drifting back toward 25% of GDP; continued fragmentation means underperformance relative to fundamentals. El Nino/climate exposure is the main exogenous risk.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
